'''bavarette†''' (bav-ạ-ret′), ''n.'' Same as ''bavette.''

'''Bavarian''' (bạ-vā′ri-ạn), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ''Bavaria'', NL. form of ML. ''Boiaria'', the country of the ''Boii'' (G. ''Baiern''), whose name is also found in ''Bohemia'', the country of the ''Boiemi'' or ''Bohemi'' (G. ''Böhmen'').] '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to Bavaria, a kingdom of southern Germany.—'''Bavarian bronze,''' {{smaller|a bronze ranging in color from a bright yellow to a copper-red. The yellow bronze contains about 82½ per cent. of copper to 17½ per cent. of tin; the red about 97 per cent. of copper to 3 per cent. of tin.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' A native or an inhabitant of Bavaria.

'''bavaroy†''' (bav′ạ-roi), ''n.'' [< F. ''Bavarois'', Bavarian.] A kind of cloak.
{{smaller block|Let the loop’d ''bavaroy'' the fop embrace.
{{right|''Gay'', Trivia, i. 53.}}}}

'''Baveno twin.''' See ''twin.''

'''baver†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''beaver''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bavette''' (bạ-vet′), ''n.'' [F., with dim. term. ''-ette'', < ''bave'' = Pr. It. ''bava'' = Sp. Pg. ''baba'' (ML. ''bava''), drivel, slaver, saliva.] '''1.''' A bib.—'''2.''' The upper part of a child’s apron turned over to serve as a bib.

'''baviant†''' (bā′vi-ạn), ''n.'' A variant form of ''baboon.''

'''bavier†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''beaver''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bavin'''<sup>1</sup> (bav′in), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [E. dial. ''bavin'', ''baven'', also ''babbin''; of obscure origin; cf. OF. ''baffe'', a bundle.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A fagot of brushwood; light and combustible wood used for kindling fires. [Now rare.]
{{smaller block|The ''Bauin'', though it burne bright, is but a blaze.
{{right|''Lyly'', Euphues, Anat. of Wit, p. 73.}}}}
readings.c1s2:
{{smaller block|If he outlasts not a hundred such crackling ''bavins'' as thou art, God and men neglect industry.
{{right|''Marston, Jonson, and Chapman'', Eastward Ho, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|About two in the morning they felt themselves almost choked with smoke, and rising, did find the fire coming up stairs: so they rose to save themselves; but that, at that time, the ''bavins'' were not on fire in the yard.
{{right|''Pepys'', Diary, III. 73.}}}}
'''2†.''' ''Milit.'', a fascine.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Resembling bavin. [Poetic.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Shallow jesters, and rash ''bavin'' wits,
Soon kindled and soon burn’d.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 2.}}}}

'''bavin<sup>1</sup>†''' (bav′in), ''v. t.'' [< ''bavin'', ''n.''] To make up into fagots.
{{smaller block|Kid or ''bavin'' them, and pitch them upon their ends to preserve them from rotting. ''Evelyn'', Sylva, p. 538.}}

'''bavin<sup>2</sup>''' (bav′in), ''n.'' [E. dial.; origin obscure.] Impure limestone. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]

'''bavin<sup>3</sup>''' (bav′in), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A name on the northeastern coast of Ireland of the ballan-wrasse.

'''Bavouism''' (ba-vö′izm), ''n.'' Same as ''Babouvism.''
{{smaller block|''Bavouism'', as Babœuf’s system was called, was thus enabled to play a rôle in French history from 1830 to 1839.
{{right|''R. T. Ely'', Fr. and Ger. Socialism, p. 34.}}}}

'''baw<sup>1</sup>''' (bâ), ''n.'' [E. dial. and Sc. (Sc. also ''ba’''), = ''ball''<sup>1</sup>.] A ball. [Prov. Eng. and Scotch.]

'''baw<sup>2</sup>''' (bâ), ''v. i.'' [E. dial., = ''bawl''<sup>1</sup>. In def. 2, cf. L. ''baubari'', bark.] '''1.''' To bawl. [Prov. Eng.]—'''2†.''' To bark. ''Topsell.''

'''baw<sup>3</sup>''' (bâ), ''interj.'' [< ME. ''baw'', ''bawe''; a natural exclamation of disgust, like ''bah.''] An ejacu-
readings.c1s3:
lation of disgust or contempt. ''Goldsmith.''

'''bawbee, baubee''' (bâ-bē′), ''n.'' [Sc., formerly also ''bawbie, baubie,'' rarely ''babie'': first mentioned in pl. ''baubeis.'' Of uncertain origin; prob. an abbr. of the name of the laird of ''Sillebawby,'' a mint-master mentioned at the date of the issuance of the bawbee, in connection with ''Atchison,'' another mint-master whose name was applied to the coin called ''atchison''; cf. also ''bodle, boddle,'' said to be named from a mint-master ''Bodwell'' or ''Bothwell.''] '''1.''' A Scotch billon coin, weighing about 29 grains troy, first issued in
[[FIGURE]]
{{c|{{smaller|Obverse. Reverse.}}}}
{{c|{{smaller|Bawbee of James V.—British Museum. (Size of the original.)}}}}
1542 by James V. of Scotland, and worth at that time 1½''d.'' Scotch. {{smaller|A half-bawbee, worth ¾''d.'' Scotch, was coined at the same time and had similar types. In Scotland the name is now given to the bronze halfpenny current throughout the British islands.}} —'''2.''' ''pl.'' Money; cash. [Scotch.]

'''bawble'''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'' See ''bauble''<sup>1</sup>.

'''bawble'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' See ''bauble''<sup>2</sup>.

readings.c2s1:
¶
'''bawchan-seed''' (bâ′chan-sēd), ''n.'' [E. Ind.; also written ''bauchee-seed.''] The seed of ''Psoralea corylifolia'', a leguminous plant of the East Indies, used by the natives as a tonic and in skin-diseases, and exported as an oil-seed.

'''bawcock''' (bâ′kok), ''n.'' [< F. ''beau coq'', fine cock: see ''beau'' and ''cock''<sup>1</sup>.] A fine fellow. [Archaic.]
{{smaller block|How now, my ''bawcock?'' {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., iii. 4.}}}}

'''bawd<sup>1</sup>''' (bâd), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''baud'', < ME. ''bawde'', ''baude'', in the earliest instance varying with ''bawdstrot'', of which ''bawd'' is prob. an abbr., being thus (prob.) indirectly, and not, as commonly supposed, directly, derived from the OF. ''baud'', bold, lively, gay. The OF. adj. is not used as a noun, and does not have the sense of the E. word. See ''bawdstrot'', and cf. ''bawdy''<sup>1</sup>, ''bawdy''<sup>2</sup>.] A procurer or procuress; a person who keeps a house of prostitution, and conducts illicit intrigues: now usually applied only to women.
{{smaller block|He [Pandarus] is named Troilus’ ''bawd.''
{{right|''Skelton'', Poems, p. 235.}}}}

'''bawd<sup>1</sup>†''' (bâd), ''v. i.'' [< ''bawd''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To pander; act as procurer or procuress.
{{smaller block|Leucippe is agent for the king’s lust, and ''bawds'' . . . for the whole court. {{right|''Spectator'', No. 266.}}}}

'''bawd<sup>2</sup>†''' (bâd), ''v. t.'' [Also spelled ''baud''; < ''bawdy''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.] To foul or dirty.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her shoone smered with tallow,
Gresed upon dyrt
That ''baudeth'' her skyrt.</poem>
{{right|''Skelton'', Poems, p. 126.}}}}
readings.c2s2:
¶
'''bawd'''<sup>3</sup> (bâd), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''baud'', perhaps abbr. from ''baudrons'', or perhaps a var. of ME. ''badde'', a cat, the name being transferred to the hare.] A hare. [In the extract there is a play on ''bawd'' in this sense and ''bawd''<sup>1</sup>.]
{{smaller block|<poem>''Mer.'' A ''bawd'', a ''bawd'' ! so ho!
''Rom.'' What hast thou found?
''Mer.'' No ''hare'', sir.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4.}}}}

'''bawd-born''' (bâd′bôrn), ''a.'' Born of a bawd; a bawd from birth. ''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2.

'''bawdekyn†''', ''n.'' See ''baudekin.''

'''bawdily''' (bâ′di-li), ''adv.'' In a bawdy manner; obscenely; lewdly.

'''bawdiness''' (bâ′di-nes), ''n.'' [< ''bawdy''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness.''] Obscenity; lewdness.

'''bawdmoney''', ''n.'' See ''baldmoney.''

'''bawdrick†''' (bâd′rik), ''n.'' See ''baldric.''

'''bawdry''' (bâd′ri), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bauderye'', < ''baude'', bawd, + ''-ry.'' Cf. OF. ''bauderie'', boldness, gayety. See ''bawd''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' The business of a bawd or procuress.—'''2.''' Illicit intercourse; fornication.
{{smaller block|We must be married, or we must live in ''bawdry.''
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' Obscenity; lewd language; smuttiness.
{{smaller block|It is most certain that barefaced ''bawdry'' is the poorest pretence to wit imaginable.{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''4†.''' Bawds collectively. ''Udall.''

'''bawdship''' (bâd′ship), ''n.'' [< ''bawd''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ship.''] The office or employment of a bawd. ''Ford.''

'''bawdstrot†''', ''n.'' [ME., also ''baudstrot'', ''baustrot'', ''baldestrot'', ''baldystrot'', < OF. *''baudestrot'', *''baldestrot'', found only in later form ''baudetrot'', prob. a cant name, and as such of obscure ori-
readings.c2s3:
gin; possibly < OF. ''baud'', ''bald'', bold (< OLG. ''bald'' = E. ''bold''), + *''strot'', < OLG. ''strotten'', *''strutten'' = Dan. ''strutte'' = MHG. G. ''strotzen'' = E. ''strut''; cf. LG. G. ''strutt'', stiff.] A bawd; a pander. ''Piers Plowman.''

¶
'''bawdy<sup>1</sup>''' (bâ′di), ''a.'' [< ''bawd''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Obscene; lewd; indecent; unchaste.

'''bawdy<sup>2</sup>†''' (bâ′di), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''baudy'', < ME. ''bawdy'', ''baudy'', dirty, appar. from a simple form *''baud'', which is not found till much later, and only as a verb (see ''bawd''<sup>2</sup>); origin unknown; cf. W. ''bawaidd'', dirty, < ''baw'', dirt, mire; F. ''boue'', mud. Not connected with ''bawdy''<sup>1</sup>, though the two words are commonly associated.] Dirty; filthy.
{{smaller block|His overslope . . . is al ''baudy'' and to-tore also.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 82.}}
Slovenly cooks, that . . . never wash their ''bawdy'' hands.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., II. 323.}}}}

'''bawdy-house''' (bâ′di-hous), ''n.'' A house of lewdness and prostitution; a house of ill-fame.

'''bawhorse''' (bâ′hôrs), ''n.'' Same as ''bathorse''.

'''bawl<sup>1</sup>''' (bâl), ''v.'' [Early mod. E. also ''ball'', ''baul'', < ME. ''bawlen'', bark, prob. < ML. ''baulare'', bark (cf. L. ''baubari'', bark); cf. mod. Icel. ''baula'' = Sw. ''böla'', low as a cow (Icel. ''baula'', a cow); cf. also Sw. ''båla'', roar, G. ''bailen'', bark, and see ''bell''<sup>2</sup>, ''bellow'', ''balk''<sup>2</sup>, etc., all prob. orig. imitative.] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To bark or howl, as a dog.—'''2.''' To cry out with a loud full sound; make vehe-
readings.c3s1:
ment or clamorous outcries, as in pain, exultation, etc.; shout. {{smaller block|That ''bawl'' for freedom in their senseless mood,
And still revolt when truth would set them free. {{right|''Milton'', Sonnets, vii.}}}} {{smaller block|Passing under Ludgate the other day, I heard a voice ''bawling'' for charity. {{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 82.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To utter or proclaim by outcry; shout out. {{smaller block|Still must I hear?—shall hoarse Fitzgerald ''bawl''
His creaking couplets in a tavern hall? {{right|''Byron'', English Bards and Scotch Reviewers.}}}} '''2.''' To cry for sale, as a hawker. {{smaller block|I saw my labours, which had cost me so much thought and watching, ''bawled'' about by the common hawkers of Grub Street. {{right|''Swift'', Bickerstaff Papers.}}}} '''bawl1''' (bâl), ''n.'' [< ''bawl1'', ''v.''] A shout at the top of one’s voice; an outcry: as, the children set up a loud ''bawl''. '''bawl2†''', ''n.'' Obsolete spelling of ''ball1''. '''bawla''' (bâ′lä), ''n.'' [Native term.] A matting made in the islands of the Pacific from the leaves of the cocoanut-palm, used for thatching. '''bawler''' (bâ′lėr), ''n.'' One who bawls. '''bawme†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''balm''. ''Chaucer.'' '''baw-money''', ''n.'' See ''bat-money''. '''bawn''' (bân), ''n.'' [< Ir. ''babhun'' = Gael. ''babhunn'' (pron. nearly as ''bawn''), an inclosure for cattle, a fortification.] '''1.''' Formerly, an outer inclosure of an Irish castle: nearly equivalent to ''bailey'' and ''outer bailey''. {{smaller|In the seventeenth century grants of government land in Ireland were made on the condition that the grantee should build a castle and bawn, the latter for the protection of the cattle of the tenants.}}
readings.c3s2:
¶
'''2.''' In modern times, in some parts of Ireland—(''a'') The cattle-yard near a farm-house. (''b'') A large house, including all its appurtenances, as offices, courtyard, etc. ''Swift.''

'''bawn''' (bân), ''v. t.'' [< ''bawn'', ''n.''] In Ireland, to surround or inclose with a bawn.

'''bawrel†''', ''n.'' [A corresponding masc. ''bawret'' is found; appar. of F. origin. Cf. ''bockerel'', ''bockeret.''] A kind of hawk. ''Phillips.''

'''bawsin''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' See ''bauson.''

'''bawsint''' (bâ′sint), ''a.'' See ''bausond.''

'''bawson''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' See ''bauson.''

'''bawtie, bawty''' (bâ′ti), ''n.'' [Sc. Cf. ''bawd''<sup>3</sup>.] In Scotland, a name for a dog, especially one of large size, and also for a hare.

'''baxa, baxea''' (bak′sä̤, -sē-ä̤), ''n.'' [L.] In ''Rom. antiq.'', a sandal or low shoe of various forms, often plaited from papyrus or palm-leaves; generally, an inexpensive foot-covering worn by the poorer classes, but also referred to as occurring in rich materials and workmanship, and specifically as the shoe of comic actors, as distinguished from the cothurnus used by tragedians.

'''baxter''' (bak′stėr), ''n.'' [Also ''backster'', < ME. ''baxter'', ''bacster'', ''bakestre'', < AS. ''bæcestre'', a baker: see ''bakester''. Hence the proper name ''Baxter'', equiv. to ''Baker''.] A baker; properly, a female baker. [Old Eng. and Scotch.]

'''Baxterian''' (baks-tē′ri-an), ''a.'' Pertaining to or propounded by Richard Baxter, a celebrated English nonconformist divine (1615–1691): as, ''Baxterian'' doctrines.
readings.c3s3:
¶
'''Baxterianism''' (baks-tē′ri-a̤n-izm), ''n.'' The doctrines of Richard Baxter, who amalgamated the Arminian doctrine of free grace with the Calvinistic doctrine of election.

'''bay'''<sup>1</sup> (bā), ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''baye'', ''baie'', < ME. ''bay'', ''baie'', a berry, esp. that of the laurel- or bay-tree, perhaps < AS. ''beg'', berry, occurring only in pl. ''beger'', ''begir'', glossed ''baccinia'', i. e. ''vaccinia'', ‘blueberries’ (see ''Vaccinium''), and in comp. ''begbeám'', lit. ‘berry-tree,’ applied both to the mulberry-tree (Gr. μορέα) and to the bramble or blackberry-bush (Gr. βάτος). But the ME. form, like MD. ''beye'', ''baeye'', a berry, a laurel-berry, agrees also with, and may have come directly from, OF. ''baie'', ''baye'', mod. F. ''baie'' = Pr. ''baia'' = Sp. ''baya'', OSp. ''baca'' = Pg. ''baga'', ''baca'' = It. ''bacca'', a berry, < L. ''bāca'', less correctly ''bacca'', a berry; cf. Lith. ''bapka'', a laurel-berry.] '''1†.''' A berry, especially of the laurel-tree.
{{smaller block|The ''bays'' or berries that it beareth.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xv. 30.}}}}

'''2.''' The laurel-tree, noble laurel, or sweet-bay, ''Laurus nobilis.'' See ''laurel.'' {{smaller|The name ''bay'' is also given to a number of trees and shrubs more or less resembling the noble laurel. See phrases below.}} Hence (like ''laurel'', and in reference to the ancient use of the laurel)—'''3.''' An honorary garland or crown bestowed as a prize for victory or excellence; also, fame or renown due to achievement or merit: in this sense used chiefly in the

{{smaller block|Leucippe is agent for the king’s lust, and ''bawds'' . . . for the whole court. {{right|''Spectator'', No. 266.}}}}

'''bawd<sup>2</sup>†''' (bâd), ''v. t.''   [Also spelled ''baud''; < ''bawdy''<sup>2</sup>, q. v.]   To foul or dirty.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her shoone smered with tallow,
Gresed upon dyrt
That ''baudeth'' her skyrt.</poem>
{{right|''Skelton'', Poems, p. 126.}}}}

'''bawd'''<sup>3</sup> (bâd), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''baud'', perhaps abbr. from ''baudrons'', or perhaps a var. of ME. ''badde'', a cat, the name being transferred to the hare.]   A hare. [In the extract there is a play on ''bawd'' in this sense and ''bawd''<sup>1</sup>.]
{{smaller block|<poem>''Mer.'' A ''bawd'', a ''bawd'' ! so ho!
''Rom.'' What hast thou found?
''Mer.'' No ''hare'', sir.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., ii. 4.}}}}

'''bawd-born''' (bâd′bôrn), ''a.'' Born of a bawd; a bawd from birth.   ''Shak.'', M. for M., iii. 2.

'''bawdekyn†''', ''n.'' See ''baudekin.''

'''bawdily''' (bâ′di-li), ''adv.'' In a bawdy manner; obscenely; lewdly.

'''bawdiness''' (bâ′di-nes), ''n.''   [< ''bawdy''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness.'']   Obscenity; lewdness.

'''bawdmoney''', ''n.'' See ''baldmoney.''

'''bawdrick†''' (bâd′rik), ''n.'' See ''baldric.''

'''bawdry''' (bâd′ri), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bauderye'', < ''baude'', bawd, + ''-ry.'' Cf. OF. ''bauderie'', boldness, gayety. See ''bawd''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The business of a bawd or procuress.—'''2.''' Illicit intercourse; fornication.
{{smaller block|We must be married, or we must live in ''bawdry.''
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, iii. 3.}}}}
'''3.''' Obscenity; lewd language; smuttiness.
{{smaller block|It is most certain that barefaced ''bawdry'' is the poorest pretence to wit imaginable.{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
'''4†.''' Bawds collectively.   ''Udall.''

'''bawdship''' (bâd′ship), ''n.''   [< ''bawd''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ship.'']   The office or employment of a bawd.   ''Ford.''

'''bawdstrot†''', ''n.''   [ME., also ''baudstrot'', ''baustrot'', ''baldestrot'', ''baldystrot'', < OF. *''baudestrot'', *''baldestrot'', found only in later form ''baudetrot'', prob. a cant name, and as such of obscure origin; possibly < OF. ''baud'', ''bald'', bold (< OLG. ''bald'' = E. ''bold''), + *''strot'', < OLG. ''strotten'', *''strutten'' = Dan. ''strutte'' = MHG. G. ''strotzen'' = E. ''strut''; cf. LG. G. ''strutt'', stiff.]   A bawd; a pander.   ''Piers Plowman.''

'''bawdy<sup>1</sup>''' (bâ′di), ''a.''   [< ''bawd''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   Obscene; lewd; indecent; unchaste.

'''bawdy<sup>2</sup>†''' (bâ′di), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''baudy'', < ME. ''bawdy'', ''baudy'', dirty, appar. from a simple form *''baud'', which is not found till much later, and only as a verb (see ''bawd''<sup>2</sup>); origin unknown; cf. W. ''bawaidd'', dirty, < ''baw'', dirt, mire; F. ''boue'', mud. Not connected with ''bawdy''<sup>1</sup>, though the two words are commonly associated.]   Dirty; filthy.
{{smaller block|His overslope . . . is al ''baudy'' and to-tore also.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Prol. to Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale, l. 82.}}}}
{{smaller block|Slovenly cooks, that . . . never wash their ''bawdy'' hands.
{{right|''Burton'', Anat. of Mel., II. 323.}}}}

'''bawdy-house''' (bâ′di-hous), ''n.'' A house of lewdness and prostitution; a house of ill-fame.

'''bawhorse''' (bâ′hôrs), ''n.'' Same as ''bathorse''.

'''bawl<sup>1</sup>''' (bâl), ''v.''   [Early mod. E. also ''ball'', ''baul'', < ME. ''bawlen'', bark, prob. < ML. ''baulare'', bark (cf. L. ''baubari'', bark); cf. mod. Icel. ''baula'' = Sw. ''böla'', low as a cow (Icel. ''baula'', a cow); cf. also Sw. ''båla'', roar, G. ''bailen'', bark, and see ''bell''<sup>2</sup>, ''bellow'', ''balk''<sup>2</sup>, etc., all prob. orig. imitative.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To bark or howl, as a dog.—'''2.''' To cry out with a loud full sound; make vehement or clamorous outcries, as in pain, exultation, etc.; shout.

{{smaller block|<poem>That ''bawl'' for freedom in their senseless mood,
And still revolt when truth would set them free.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', Sonnets, vii.}}}}

{{smaller block|Passing under Ludgate the other day, I heard a voice ''bawling'' for charity.
{{right|''Steele'', Spectator, No. 82.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To utter or proclaim by outcry; shout out.

{{smaller block|<poem>Still must I hear?—shall hoarse Fitzgerald ''bawl''
His creaking couplets in a tavern hall?</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', English Bards and Scotch Reviewers.}}}}

'''2.''' To cry for sale, as a hawker.

{{smaller block|I saw my labours, which had cost me so much thought and watching, ''bawled'' about by the common hawkers of Grub Street.
{{right|''Swift'', Bickerstaff Papers.}}}}

'''bawl<sup>1</sup>''' (bâl), ''n.''   [< ''bawl<sup>1</sup>'', ''v.'']   A shout at the top of one’s voice; an outcry: as, the children set up a loud ''bawl''.

'''bawl<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'' Obsolete spelling of ''ball<sup>1</sup>''.

'''bawla''' (bâ′lä), ''n.''   [Native term.]   A matting made in the islands of the Pacific from the leaves of the cocoanut-palm, used for thatching.

'''bawler''' (bâ′lėr), ''n.'' One who bawls.

'''bawme†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''balm''.   ''Chaucer.''

'''baw-money''', ''n.'' See ''bat-money''.

'''bawn''' (bân), ''n.''   [< Ir. ''babhun'' = Gael. ''babhunn'' (pron. nearly as ''bawn''), an inclosure for cattle, a fortification.]   '''1.''' Formerly, an outer inclosure of an Irish castle: nearly equivalent to ''bailey'' and ''outer bailey''. {{smaller|In the seventeenth century grants of government land in Ireland were made on the condition that the grantee should build a castle and bawn, the latter for the protection of the cattle of the tenants.}}

'''2.''' In modern times, in some parts of Ireland—(''a'') The cattle-yard near a farm-house. (''b'') A large house, including all its appurtenances, as offices, courtyard, etc.   ''Swift.''

'''bawn''' (bân), ''v. t.''   [< ''bawn'', ''n.'']   In Ireland, to surround or inclose with a bawn.

'''bawrel†''', ''n.''   [A corresponding masc. ''bawret'' is found; appar. of F. origin. Cf. ''bockerel'', ''bockeret.'']   A kind of hawk.   ''Phillips.''

'''bawsin''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' See ''bauson.''

'''bawsint''' (bâ′sint), ''a.'' See ''bausond.''

'''bawson''', ''n.'' and ''a.'' See ''bauson.''

'''bawtie, bawty''' (bâ′ti), ''n.''   [Sc. Cf. ''bawd''<sup>3</sup>.]   In Scotland, a name for a dog, especially one of large size, and also for a hare.

'''baxa, baxea''' (bak′sä̤, -sē-ä̤), ''n.''   [L.]   In ''Rom. antiq.'', a sandal or low shoe of various forms, often plaited from papyrus or palm-leaves; generally, an inexpensive foot-covering worn by the poorer classes, but also referred to as occurring in rich materials and workmanship, and specifically as the shoe of comic actors, as distinguished from the cothurnus used by tragedians.

'''baxter''' (bak′stėr), ''n.''   [Also ''backster'', < ME. ''baxter'', ''bacster'', ''bakestre'', < AS. ''bæcestre'', a baker: see ''bakester''. Hence the proper name ''Baxter'', equiv. to ''Baker''.]   A baker; properly, a female baker. [Old Eng. and Scotch.]

'''Baxterian''' (baks-tē′ri-an), ''a.'' Pertaining to or propounded by Richard Baxter, a celebrated English nonconformist divine (1615–1691): as, ''Baxterian'' doctrines.

'''Baxterianism''' (baks-tē′ri-a̤n-izm), ''n.'' The doctrines of Richard Baxter, who amalgamated the Arminian doctrine of free grace with the Calvinistic doctrine of election.

'''bay'''<sup>1</sup> (bā), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. also ''baye'', ''baie'', < ME. ''bay'', ''baie'', a berry, esp. that of the laurel- or bay-tree, perhaps < AS. ''beg'', berry, occurring only in pl. ''beger'', ''begir'', glossed ''baccinia'', i. e. ''vaccinia'', ‘blueberries’ (see ''Vaccinium''), and in comp. ''begbeám'', lit. ‘berry-tree,’ applied both to the mulberry-tree (Gr. μορέα) and to the bramble or blackberry-bush (Gr. βάτος). But the ME. form, like MD. ''beye'', ''baeye'', a berry, a laurel-berry, agrees also with, and may have come directly from, OF. ''baie'', ''baye'', mod. F. ''baie'' = Pr. ''baia'' = Sp. ''baya'', OSp. ''baca'' = Pg. ''baga'', ''baca'' = It. ''bacca'', a berry, < L. ''bāca'', less correctly ''bacca'', a berry; cf. Lith. ''bapka'', a laurel-berry.]   '''1†.''' A berry, especially of the laurel-tree.
{{smaller block|The ''bays'' or berries that it beareth.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, xv. 30.}}}}

'''2.''' The laurel-tree, noble laurel, or sweet-bay, ''Laurus nobilis.'' See ''laurel.'' {{smaller|The name ''bay'' is also given to a number of trees and shrubs more or less resembling the noble laurel. See phrases below.}} Hence (like ''laurel'', and in reference to the ancient use of the laurel)—'''3.''' An honorary garland or crown bestowed as a prize for victory or excellence; also, fame or renown due to achievement or merit: in this sense used chiefly in the<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
